case_name: R. v. Hahamovitch Kosher Imports Inc.
text:
REJB 1998-08081 - Texte
intégral

CITATION: R. v. Hahamovitch Kosher
Imports Inc.

Cour
du Québec
(Chambre criminelle et pénale)

CANADA

PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC

DISTRICT DE  de Montréal

NO : 500-01-023026-922

DATE :  1998-01-07

EN PRÉSENCE DE :

Bernard Grenier
, J.C.Q.

The Queen

Prosecutor

v.

Hahamovitch Kosher Imports Inc.

Defendant

Bernard Grenier, J.C.Q.:-

1
The Defendant company is
charged with the following accusations:

13. Le ou vers le
11 février 1992 avait en sa possession pour la vente dans son
établissement commercial du 6600 Thimens à Ville Saint-Laurent
(Québec), des aliments à savoir, 288 emballages de «oat
bran crunchy snacks cookies» de marque «Sun Valley» 340g,
comportant sur l'emballage, l'allégation «no cholesterol»
sans déclaration de la teneur en polyinsaturés, en
monoinsaturés et en saturés exprimée en grammes par
portion déterminée, contrairement aux dispositions de l'article
5(1) (2) de la Loi sur les aliments et drogues L.R.C. 1985 CH. 27 ainsi que
l'article B.01.303(1)(a) des règlements sur les aliments et drogues
commettant ainsi l'infraction punissable sur déclaration sommaire de
culpabilité prévue à l'article 31(a) de ladite Loi.

14. Le ou vers le
11 février 1992 avait en sa possession pour la vente dans son
établissement commercial situé au 6600 Thimens à Ville
Saint-Laurent (Québec), des aliments à savoir, 288 emballages de
«oat bran crunchy snacks (cookies)» de marque «Sun
Valley» 340g, comportant sur l'emballage l'allégation «low
in saturated fats» sans la déclaration de la teneur en
polyinsaturés, en monoinsaturés et en saturés
exprimée en grammes par portion déterminée et de la teneur
en cholestérol exprimée en milligrammes par portion
déterminée, contrairement aux dispositions de l'
article 5(1)
(2)
de la
Loi sur les aliments et drogues L.R.C. 1985 CH» F.27
ainsi que
l'article B.01.303(1) (a) des règlements sur les aliments et drogues
commettant ainsi une infraction punissable sur déclaration sommaire de
culpabilité prévue à l'article 31(a) de ladite Loi.

15. Le ou vers le
11 février 1992, avait en sa possession pour la vente dans son
établissement commercial situé aux 6600 Thimens à Ville
Saint-Laurent (Québec), des aliments à savoir 168 emballages de
«bite size snackers (unsalted tops) de marque «Lieber's»
283g, comportant sur l'emballage l'allégation «low sodium»
et dont l'étiquette mentionne 55 mg par demi-once alors que la teneur en
sodium excède la quantité maximale exigée de 40 mg de
sodium par 100 g de l'aliment, contrairement aux dispositions de l'
article 5(1)

(2) de la
Loi sur les aliments et drogues L.R.C. 1985 CH. F 27
ainsi que
l'article B.24.003 (e) ainsi que l'article B.24.008 (b) et (e) du
règlement sur les aliments et drogues, commettant ainsi l'infraction
punissable sur déclaration sommaire de culpabilité prévue
à l'article 31(a) de ladite Loi.

2
Defence
counsel challenged the constitutionality of sections B.01.303 (1) (a), section
B.24.003 (e) and B.24.008 (b) (e) of the regulations adopted under the
Food
and Drugs Act
(L.R.C. 1985 C. 27) and of the same regulations, on the
ground that they violated the freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by
section 2 (a) of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedom
.

3
On the 18
th
of January 1996,
I concluded that the impugned legislation does violate the freedom guaranteed
by
section 2 (a)
of the
Charter
. The next step was to determine whether under

section 1
of the Charter, the violation was a reasonable limit prescribed by
law that could be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

4
The
Prosecution presented Dr. Margaret Cheney in support of its position that the
violation was a reasonable limit. On behalf of the Defendant, I heard the
testimony of Dr. Ian Craig Monroe and Mr. Michael Zimlichman. Dr. Cheney works
in the field of nutrition evaluation for Health and Welfare Canada, whereas Dr.
Monroe is a consultant and a scientist. Both testified on the history, aims and
purposes of the regulations dealing with cholesterol and sodium, which are
under attack in this case. Dr. Cheney and Dr. Monroe are very impressive
witnesses, with undeniable competence and enviable credentials.

5
The
relevant legislation reads as follows:

5.(1) No person
shall label, package, treat, process, sell or advertise any food in a manner
that is false, misleading or deceptive or is likely to create an erroneous
impression regarding its character, value, quantity, composition, merit or
safety.

(2) An article of
food that is not labelled or packaged as required by, or is labelled or
packaged contrary to, the regulations shall be deemed to be labelled or
packaged contrary to subsection (1).

B.01.303(1) No
person shall, on the label of or in any advertisement for a food, other than a
formulated liquid diet, a meal replacement for weight reduction diets, a human
milk substitute or a food represented as containing a human milk substitute,
make a statement or claim relating to the fatty acid or cholesterol content of
the food unless a declaration is made of the content of fat, cis-methylene
interrupted polyunsaturated fatty acids, cismonoun-saturated fatty acids and
saturated fatty acids, expressed in grams per serving of stated size.

.24.003(1) No
person shall label, package, sell or advertise a food in a manner likely to
create an impression that it is a food for special dietary use unless the food
is:

(e) a low sodium
food that meets the requirements contained in section B.24.008.

B.24.008 a low
sodium food is a food that, when ready to serve, contains

(b) not more than
40 miligrams of sodium per 100 grams of food, in the case of foods other than
those described in paragraphs (c) and (d).

6
From the
wording of
section 5
of the
Food and Drugs Act
and of the
above-mentioned regulations, I conclude that the legislation under attack has
two distinct goals. First, it is aimed at ensuring that consumers will not be
deceived or misinformed concerning the content of the product which they are
buying. The second goal is to help people with dietary problems to buy only
food suitable to their situation, and to avoid any product that may cause them
health problems.

7
The
evidence also shows that the producers chose to put the mentions «no
cholesterol», «low in saturated fats» and «low
sodium» on the labels. From my understanding of the evidence, there was
no obligation to print these advertisements on the boxes or cans of food sold
to the consumers. According to the Prosecution, if producers choose to mention
the words «no cholesterol», «low in saturated fats» and
«low sodium» on the labels, or if distributors choose to sell these
products on the Canadian market, they should abide by the appropriate
regulations.

8
The
evidence also shows that the cookies and snackers described in the accusations
were to be sold for Passover to a relatively limited segment of the Jewish
population. Because the Canadian market for these types of foods is relatively
small, it was decided that it would be too costly to produce them here instead
of importing them from the United States or Israel. As Mr. Zimlichman said in
his testimony, the products we are dealing with in this case represent a very
small portion of the food that he imports on a yearly basis.

The Oakes Test

9
In
R. v.
Oakes
(1986)
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 1 S.C.R., 103), the Supreme Court of Canada proposed a
framework of analysis under
section 1
of the
Charter
. The Court said that the
onus of proving that a limitation on a Charter right is reasonable and
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society rests upon the party
seeking to uphold the limitation. The burden of proof is the balance of
probabilities. The analysis must be based on the following criteria:

1. The objective to
be served by the measures limiting a
Charter
right must be sufficiently
important, at least relating to societal concerns which are pressing and
substantial in a free and democratic society, to warrant overriding a
constitutionally protected right or freedom.

2. The means must
be reasonable and demonstrably justified in proportion to the importance of the
objective. The proportionality test involves three components:

a) the measures
must be fair and not arbitrary, carefully designed to achieve the objective in
question and rationally connected to that objective.

b) the means should
impair the
Charter
right as little as possible.

3. There must be a
proportionality between the effects of the limiting measure and the objective.

A. Societal Concerns which are Pressing
and Substantial

10
The
regulations under attack advance concerns which are pressing and substantial in
a free and democratic society. Their goal is to make sure that consumers who
want to read the labels are able to determine the exact contents of the
product, so that, if they have a dietary or health problem, they will be able
to avoid food which is not suitable to them.

11
One has to
keep in mind that the level of fat can have an impact on cardio-vascular
diseases which, in passing, represent 38% of all deaths in Canada.

12
As far as
sodium is concerned, its consumption may have deleterious effects on persons
suffering from hypertension and kidney diseases. The regulations dealing with
low sodium are aimed at persons on sodium restricted diets. They provide that a
food product which purports to be low in sodium may not contain more than 40mg
of sodium per 100 grams of food.

13
The
importance of protecting health and the necessity to foster fair and honest
information about the composition of food products, lead me to the conclusion
that the impugned regulations relate to societal concerns which are pressing and
substantial in a free and democratic society.

B. Proportionality

14
Are the
means adopted by the legislation reasonable and demonstrably justified, in
proportion to the importance of the objective? I will deal with this question
in three steps, as suggested by the Supreme court of Canada in
Oakes
.

a) Rational connection

15
At first
glance, it would appear that regulations providing for a detailed description
of the content in fat of food claiming to have no cholesterol or to be low in
saturated fat, is rationally connected to the aim of protecting public health
and promoting consumer protection. The same applies to legislation which sets a
limit of 40mg of sodium per 100gr of food for any food claiming to be low in
sodium where, in fact, the proportion of sodium is higher than the ceiling
imposed by the legislation.

16
Defence
counsel argues that most consumers do not understand what they read on the
labels of food products. He relies on the testimony of Dr. Monroe to that
effect. Where is the rational connection between the goal pursued and the means
adopted if people do not understand the content of the label?

17
Counsel
for the prosecution says, for his part, that according to a study prepared by
Debra Reid and published in 1992 under the title
Consumer Use and
Understanding of Nutrition Information of Food Package Labels
, 46% of
respondents in a research study said they understand nutritional claims very
well, compared to ingredient lists (38%) and nutrition panels (34%) (see
Brandeis Brief of Legislative Fact Evidence presented by the Prosecution, tab.
7, p. XIII).

18
It is fair
to assume that many citizens who venture to read the labels on boxes or cans of
food are no further advanced because of the very technical nature of the
information. This being said, the information is readily available for those
who are able to decipher technical terms, or who wish to consult a specialist
to know if eating the product in question poses a risk to their health. It is
true that we live in an highly regulated society and that most citizens are
ignorant of the vast majority of the regulations which govern them. Those who
know of the existence of some of the regulations will not understand them
easily, unless they are specialized in the field covered by those regulations.

19

Section 19

of the
Criminal Code
provides that ignorance of the law is no defence. With
that principle in mind, it would be illogical to declare a law inoperative on
the ground that it is not understood by a portion of the population, except if
the law is ruled void for vagueness according to the criteria set forth in
R.
v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society
(1992)
1992 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R., 606).

20
If a
Canadian citizen charged with a criminal offence is not allowed to plead in
defence that he or she did not know the law allegedly violated, it cannot be
argued that sections of a law or of a regulation, such as those with which we
are dealing here, are inoperative on the ground that they are not easily
understood. It is likely that several people do not know or understand many
aspects of the legislation which they are presumed to know for the purposes of
criminal law. There must be consistency in the interpretation and application
of the law.

21
Does this
problem of communication take away the «raison d'être» of the
regulations? Does it make them, if not irrelevant, at least devoid of any
logical rationality, considering the goals which this legislation wishes to
attain? The answer is no. It is important that people who are at risk in any aspect
of regulated human activity be in a position to know where the risks are, and
the limits to what they might permit themselves to consume.

22
Defence
counsel also pointed out, following Dr. Monroe's testimony, that regulation
B.01.303(1)(a) does not require the level of transfatty acid to be mentioned on
a label. Does this mean that the regulation is not rationally connected to the
protection of health and consumer's right to be informed? The answer is no. The
law could contain even more requirements as to the content of food, but the
fact that it does not in no way deprives it of a rational connection with the
goal that it wishes to achieve.

23
Counsel
for the defence also noted that there is no exception in the impugned
regulations for specialty foods, contrary to regulations on bilingualism which
contain such exceptions. Does that mean that there is no rational connection
between the measures and the objective? Once again the answer is no.

24
In my
opinion, the absence of any exception in the legislation under attack is
understandable because of the potential danger for public health in allowing
foods products to be sold when these products do not reveal adequate
information about their compositional content. On the other hand, the fact that
a label is not bilingual does not create the same risk for public health, as
long as it contains at least one of the two official languages of Canada.
Requirements addressing the language used on a box or a can of food have to do
with the means of communicating a message, not about the message itself.
Requirements about information concerning the content of food have to do with
the message.

25
The
legislation under attack passes the rational connection test.

b) Minimal impairment

26
Does the
legislation infringe the
Charter
right as little as possible? Before dealing
with the issue, it is appropriate to quote from a decision of Supreme Court of
Canada,
CBC v New Brunswick (A.G.)
(1996)
1996 CanLII 184 (SCC)
, 3S.C.R. 480, p. 509:

... if the law
falls within a range of reasonable alternatives, the Courts will not find it
overbroad merely because they can conceive of an alternative which might better
tailor objective to infringement.

27
In the
case of
R. v Edwards Books and Art Ltd
(1986)
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, 2 S.C.R. 713 ), Justice La
Forest made the following comments:

Let me first
underline what is mentioned in the Chief Justice's judgment, that in describing
the criteria comprising the proportionality requirement, the Court has been
careful to avoid rigid and inflexible standards. That seems to me to be
essential. Given that the objective is of pressing and substantial concern, the
Legislature must be allowed adequate scope to achieve that objective. It must
be remembered that the business of government is a practical one. The
Constitution must be applied on a realistic basis having regard to the nature
of the particular area sought to be regulated and not on an abstract
theoretical plane...

By the foregoing, I
do not mean to suggest that this Court should, as a general rule, defer to
legislative judgments when those judgments trench upon rights considered
fundamental in a free and democratic society. Quite the contrary, I would have
thought the
Charter
established the opposite regime. On the other hand, having
accepted the importance of the legislative objective, one must in the present
context recognize that if the legislative goal is to be achieved, it will
inevitably be achieved to the detriment of some. Moreover, attempts to protect
the rights of one group will also inevitably impose burdens on the rights of other
groups. There is no perfect scenario in which the rights of all can be equally
protected.

In seeking to
achieve a goal that is demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society,
therefore, a legislature must be given reasonable room to manoeuvre to meet
these conflicting pressures. Of course, what is reasonable will vary with the
context. Regard must be had to the nature of the interest infringed and to the
legislative scheme sought to be implemented. (pp. 794–795)

28
It is
worth pointing out that the decision to print words like «no
cholesterol», «low in saturated fats» and «low
sodium» on labels is purely voluntary. The regulations apply only if the
manufacturer decides to make these claims. Only then are the requirements about
compositional content triggered by the regulations..

29
In her
testimony, Dr. Cheney said that the authorities chose to use prohibitions
instead of guidelines because they felt that prohibitions have more
«teeth» and more clout. She also said that, at one point, Canada
had adopted a low sodium maximum of 10mg per food serving. Later on the level
was increased to 40mg. Other countries have a higher ceiling than Canada.

30
In
RJR
McDonald Inc. v. Canada (A.G.)
(1995)
1995 CanLII 64 (SCC)
, 3 S.C.R. 199 ), the Supreme Court of
Canada struck down the
Tobacco Products Control Act
which broadly
prohibited all advertising and promotion of tobacco products and the sale of a
tobacco product unless its package included prescribed unattributed health
warnings and the list of toxic constituents. The legislative scheme targeted
three distinct categories of commercial activity: advertising, promotion and
labelling.

31
The
Supreme Court came to the conclusion that the prohibition on advertising and
promotion under the Act infringed the Appelant's right to freedom of expression
guaranteed by section 2b of the
Charter
. That case must be distinguished from
the present situation because of the fact that the impugned regulations apply
only if a manufactured chooses to include certains words like «no cholesterol»
etc. on a label. In
R.J.R. McDonald
, the law forced distributors to
print the warning on tobacco products.

32
I take
into consideration, as counsel for the prosecution writes in his memorandum,
that «the legislative construction and objective of the provision are so
far removed from religious concerns, that it could not have been reasonably
conceived by the legislative drafters that this provision could possibly affect
the right of persons of the Jewish faith to eat certain Kosher food products».

33
The goal
of promoting public health and consumer protection has to be balanced against
the effect the regulations have on a relatively limited number of people who,
for religious reasons, choose to eat only certain types of food at Passover.
The regulations do not hamper the practice of religion by all members of the
Jewish faith. It relates to the capacity of certain people to buy a special
category of cookies or snackers.

34
The
decision not to produce in Canada the Passover foods involved in the present
case is purely economic. Due to the small nature of the Canadian market, it was
decided to import those foods from the United States or Israel, instead of
producing them here.

35
Some may
feel that the requirements imposed by the regulations adopted under the
Food
and Drugs Act
are questionable and that other avenues could have been
envisaged; for instance the use of guidelines or of a 1-800 line giving
information about the contents of certain products. Some may believe that a
limit of 40mg for low sodium products is too low or too high. The real question
is whether there is anything arbitrary in the regulations under attack. The
answer is no. The judiciary should not declare a piece of legislation
inoperative under
section 1
of the
Charter
based on a mere preference for a
particular policy as opposed to another, unless the policy in question is
arbitrary or otherwise unacceptable.

36
Judicial
deference to decisions made by the Legislator must not lead to a form of
servility or a slavishness. As Madame Justice McLaughlin wrote in
RJR
McDonald
,:

Context is
essential in determining legislative objective and proportionality, but it
cannot be carried to the extreme of treating the challenged law as a unique
socio-economic phenomenon, of which Parliament is the best judge. This would be
to undercut the obligation on Parliament to justify limitations which it places
on
Charter
rights and would be to substitute ad hoc judicial descretion for the
reasoned demonstration required by the Charter. (p.331)

... To carry
judicial deference to the point of accepting Parliament's view simply on the
basis that the problem is serious and the solution difficult, would be to
diminish the role of the Courts in the constitutional process and to weaken the
structure of rights upon which our constitution and our nation is founded.
(p.332-333)

37
Everything
is a question of balance and common sense.

38
Dr. Monroe
testified to the effect that some of the standards adopted in the legislation
under attack may be changed to achieve harmonization with American standards,
following the adoption of the
North American Free Trade Agreement
. Even
if the standards may eventually be modified in the future, the fact remains
that at the time of the alleged offences, the law said what it said. My
decision must be rendered according to the law which was applicable at the
time.

39
Counsel
for the prosecution reviewed the legislation from various jurisdictions
concerning cholesterol, saturated fats, and low sodium claims. I do not intend
to reproduce every figure mentioned in his memorandum, Suffice it to say that I
agree with his conclusion that the provisions under attack fall well within a
range of reasonable alternatives, when compared to the situations in other
countries.

40
The
defendant pointed out that the authorities have, in the past, refrained from
laying charges following the sale of Passover food that did not meet all
requirements of the regulations under attack. The defendant added that this
attitude of tolerance, adopted by government representatives, is indicative of
the exceptional situation which the acquiring of Passover food represents for
some members of the Jewish faith.

41
The
authorities may have chosen, in the exercise of the discretion, not to enforce
the law for reasons to which I am not privy.

42
The
constitutionality of legislation has nothing to do with prosecutorial policies.
The fact that the authorities decide not to lay charges under a law does not
mean that the law in question is invalid. It is for the courts to rule whether
a law is inoperative under the
Charter
.

43
I conclude
that the impugned legislation passes the minimal impairment test.

C. Proportionality

44
Is there
proportionality between the effects of the limiting measure and the objective
that the legislation tries to reach? It is not necessary to repeat what was
said about the voluntary nature of the nutritional claims made by the
distributors of the cookies and snackers involved in the present case. Neither
is it necessary to repeat what was said about the limited infringement on the
right of those members of the Jewish faith who buy certain Kosher foods for
Passover, as opposed to a much broader interference with the practice of their
religion as a whole.

45
The
restrictions on trade barriers imposed by the regulations are also of minimal
consequence.

46
I am of
the opinion that the advantages, in terms of protection of the health of
consumers and of their right to be well informed about their choice of food,
far outweigh the disavantages for those who would be prevented to buy the
products involved in this case.

47
The
legislation under attack passes the proportionality test.

Conclusion

48
The
Prosecution has proved on the balance of probalities that the restrictions to
freedom of religion which, I have decided, derive from the application of
regulations B.01.303(1)(a) and B.24003.(1)(e) and B.24.008(b), are reasonable
limits which can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

Bernard
Grenier, J.C.Q.

Me Gilles Villeneuve
, Crown Prosecutor.

Me Paul Nadler
, Attorney for the Defence.
